newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco industry agrees to landmark $368.5 billion pact.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco industry agrees to landmark $368.5 billion pact.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The tobacco industry, which has never spent a cent on damages, agreed on Friday to pay a staggering $368.5 billion and submit to federal regulation in a landmark settlement that was once unimaginable.

The proposed agreement marks a severe defeat for the proud and powerful industry that has boasted for decades it would never settle a smoking case and has denied that cigarettes are addictive or cause lung cancer.
Facing the prospect of massive and unprecedented litigation, the industry said it was swallowing a "bitter pill" with legislative and regulatory provisions with which it does not necessarily agree.

The agreement is by far the largest ever involving an industry and concludes three months of negotiations that grew from an innovative lawsuit filed in 1994 by Mississippi's attorney general without the knowledge of his governor.
Although the parties have reached an agreement, the proposed settlement now faces what could be a rocky approval process before the White House and Congress.

Among the proposal's key provisions are that the industry will be regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, will sharply curtail advertising and marketing of cigarettes and will admit the dangers of using tobacco.
The industry has also agreed to be penalized if youth smoking is not reduced and to pay for smoking cessation programs.
"We are here today to announce what ... is the most historic public health achievement in history," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told a news conference.

"We wanted this industry to have to change the way they do business, and we have done that. We wanted the industry to stop marketing their products to our kids, and we have come up with a comprehensive plan that will do that," Moore said. "We wanted to do something that would punish this industry for their past misconduct, and we have done that."

Although the tobacco industry is facing hundreds of class-action and individual lawsuits, many legal experts believe the industry felt most threatened by lawsuits filed by 40 state attorneys general seeking to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Attorneys general are the highest ranking legal officers in each state.

The states have maintained that a key goal of their lawsuits was to reduce youth smoking, and indeed a large part of the proposal is aimed at just that. For example, the proposal prevents the industry from using cartoon characters or human images in its advertising.

"The Marlboro Man will be riding into the sunset on Joe Camel," said Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth. "Joe Camel and the Marlboro Man will move to the same chapter of our nation's history as asbestos, the Corvair and the Edsel, and you know that's exactly where they belong."
In addition to paying for health programs, the huge fund will be used to reimburse states and to fund awards given in individual lawsuits.

Because the size of the fund is aimed at punishing the industry for past wrongdoing, individual claimants will only be able to seek punitive damages for future egregious conduct. The agreement also bars future class-action lawsuits.
Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Senior Vice President Steven Parrish said the industry disagreed with some elements of the proposed settlement.
"The proposal is a bitter pill because our companies have made concessions that were extremely difficult," he said.
"But on balance, this plan is preferable to a continuation of a decades-long controversy that has failed to produce a constructive outcome for anyone."
The agreement was announced at packed news conference in the nation's capital and was immediately hailed by President Bill Clinton, who said he would appoint a task force to review its terms.

"We must now carefully consider whether approving this proposed settlement will protect the public health," he said in a statement that named Donna Shalala, Health and Human Services secretary, and White House aide Bruce Reed to head up the review.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said it is expected the review will take a "matter of weeks" not months.

One of the biggest concessions by the industry is the recognition that the FDA has regulatory power over tobacco products, including the authority to reduce the levels of nicotine and eventually eliminate it.
Under the deal, the FDA would have the authority to ban nicotine after 12 years.

It also would require FDA approval of all ingredients in tobacco products and standards for reducing harmful components, including nicotine. The proposed agreement mandates testing of ingredients and safety assessments.

The tobacco industry would also give the FDA all research it conducts. The agreement also would impose penalties for any violations that are 10 times those facing other companies regulated by the FDA, the attorneys general said.
